title: BalancerPoolerV2.migrateMint mints id-6 at NEW_NFT_INDEX=6 with no validation that NFTMinterV2.configs[6] still points at the intended dispatcher; an in-flight replaceDispatcher(6, ...) silently re-routes migration receipts to a different dispatcher
description:
migrateMint passes `NEW_NFT_INDEX = 6` to NFTMinterV2.mintFor. NFTMinterV2.mintFor validates `configs[index].dispatcher != address(0)` but does NOT validate that the dispatcher at that index is *this* dispatcher (the one calling migrateMint). The mapping `configs[6].dispatcher` is owner-mutable via NFTMinterV2.replaceDispatcher(6, newDispatcher). The token id minted is `6` regardless of which dispatcher currently sits at that index; from the recipient's perspective, the token id is what determines all future claim semantics (uri(), tokenIdToDispatcher mapping for image / name / description, any future redemption logic that consults `tokenIdToDispatcher[6]`).

A narrow but realistic race:

1. The new BalancerPoolerV2 deployment is registered at index 6 via `NFTMinterV2.replaceDispatcher(6, newPooler)` per the design note in L37-L40.
2. Holders of id-4 begin sending migrateMint transactions. Some are pending in the mempool.
3. The owner sends `NFTMinterV2.replaceDispatcher(6, otherDispatcher)` for any reason — a configuration fix, a deployment of an updated dispatcher, a panicked rollback. Replacement is permitted with no quiescence check.
4. Pending migrateMint transactions land. Each one still calls `mintFor(6, recipient)` — index 6 is still registered, configs[6].dispatcher is now `otherDispatcher`, and the mint succeeds. The migrated id-6 NFTs are now bound to `otherDispatcher` for all metadata and (if a future story adds it) all redemption semantics.
5. The user expected an id-6 NFT redeemable against newPooler; they receive an id-6 NFT redeemable against otherDispatcher. The on-chain token id is the same; the dispatcher behind it has been silently swapped.

The attack surface is narrow because (a) it requires a same-block or same-window replaceDispatcher action by the owner, and (b) the contract framing already says 'owner is trusted' (project KI #4). But the migrateMint code makes the situation worse than the paid mint path: in NFTMinterV2._executeMint (paid), the user pays and dispatches against the *current* dispatcher in the same atomic call, so the user knows what they paid for. In migrateMint the user pays nothing and the dispatcher behind the freshly minted token id is not even read inside the migration call — there is no on-chain assertion that the id-6 they receive is bound to the dispatcher they were promised.

Fix is cheap: assert at the top of migrateMint that NFTMinterV2.configs(NEW_NFT_INDEX).dispatcher == address(this). If a replaceDispatcher slipped in, migrateMint reverts cleanly and pending txs do not silently re-route.
exploit_path:
1. Owner deploys new BalancerPoolerV2 instance P and registers it at index 6: `NFTMinterV2.replaceDispatcher(6, P)`. Public announcement: 'id-4 migration is live, holders receive id-6 redeemable against P.'
2. Alice queues a tx: `P.migrateMint(10, alice)`.
3. Before Alice's tx lands, owner (or compromised owner key, or a fast governance vote with low quorum) calls `NFTMinterV2.replaceDispatcher(6, Q)` where Q is a different dispatcher (an attacker-deployed dispatcher returning misleading metadata, or a 'placeholder' the operator did not intend to expose to migrators).
4. Alice's tx lands. The id-4 burns from alice succeed. The 10 mintFor(6, alice) calls succeed because configs[6].dispatcher = Q != 0. Alice now holds 10 id-6 NFTs whose ` tokenIdToDispatcher[6]` resolves to Q. NFTMinterV2.uri(6) returns Q's name/image/description, not P's. Any downstream redemption that consults tokenIdToDispatcher[6] will treat alice's holdings as bound to Q.
5. Alice has no on-chain warning. ClaimMintedFor(alice, 6, P) fires (the minter argument is `msg.sender` of mintFor, i.e. P, the OLD pooler that called migrateMint). The event suggests 'P minted the token,' which is true, but the resolved dispatcher behind the token id is Q.

The scenario is largely a centralisation / owner-trust scenario, but the migrateMint code makes the situation worse because the function does not pin the destination dispatcher to itself.
mainnet_realism_check: Pure on-chain logic. replaceDispatcher is mainnet-callable by the owner with no timelock. Mempool race conditions of this shape are realistic on Ethereum mainnet given the typical 1-block-finality / mempool exposure window.
recommendation: Add the invariant `require(NFTMinterV2(minter).tokenIdToDispatcher(NEW_NFT_INDEX) == address(this), "BalancerPoolerV2: migration target replaced");` (or equivalent assertion against configs(NEW_NFT_INDEX).dispatcher) at the top of migrateMint. If the dispatcher behind index 6 has been swapped, migrations revert until the operator either (a) re-points index 6 back to this dispatcher, or (b) deliberately closes the migration via the lifecycle marker recommended in RAW-003. This costs one SLOAD per migrateMint call and removes the silent-redirect class of failure entirely.
